strategy.summary: Family-owned welding/sheet-metal shop, our single approved source for the HN 100 base frame (tooling ours). Sound finances, moderate dependency on us. It has cut price repeatedly since 2023 and historically settles below its own ask. Steel and labour indices now rise, so a 2027 increase request is likely. Its one explicit wish is faster payment against a cash discount; we pay slightly late on most invoices, which is its legitimate grievance. Delivery is below the contract target but above peers and improving; ppm has risen above peers. Evidence on persona and cost structure is thin: no should-cost, no rival quotes.
strategy.decision_maker: Unknown; likely owner or managing director of a family GmbH with a short decision path (inference, not documented).

persona.style: orderly, planning-focused, polite; raises practical asks (early call-offs, faster payment)
other_traits: values cash and working capital without financial stress
has already conceded price over several years

needs.detail: Asked us to pay within a short period in exchange for a cash discount; request appears unused so far. Likely working-capital preference, not distress.
Punctual payment: we pay most invoices a few days late, with no discounts taken.
Plans its plant tightly (shutdown notice, call-off deadline); shared, stable forecasts and binding volume help it.
Steel and labour cost drivers are rising after years of price cuts; it will want recovery or at least no further cut.
Forecast slightly above recent orders; binding volume is a modest plus for a shop of this size.

constraints.detail: Only approved source for the part; switching needs requalification despite our tooling ownership.
Price fixed per calendar year; changes need written notice ahead of year end. Contract auto-extends unless terminated with notice.
Rising steel and labour costs are real and checkable; further cuts lack cost justification and no should-cost exists.

levers.why: Its own cash request; offering faster payment answers it and buys price restraint.
Anchors talks at the current price.
Shared, slightly higher forecast can be committed as binding for a price step.
Rolling ppm above peer median and up from zero; checkable counterweight to an increase.
Small checkable power-cost offset; fresh fact for a later round.
An increase without timely notice has no contractual basis.
Below contract target; use calmly as late filler, acknowledging improvement.
Part-specific complaints; supports ppm commitment rather than big cut.
Our tooling makes a move feasible; state as fact only if it stonewalls.

trades.why: It explicitly wants faster payment; trade shorter payment for a price step, ideally in the final round.
Binding volume within our real need gives planning security it values.
A longer commitment is worth something to a family shop; 24 months captures it.
Rising ppm; a tighter target addresses our real cost without squeezing price.
If an increase is unavoidable, a later start at slightly higher price may cost us less.
Avoid a steel clause while the index is rising; accept only if it insists and priced well below fixed.

price_view.reasoning: Price already cut substantially since 2023 while steel and labour rose; drivers now justify a modest increase. History shows settlements well below its asks, so holding flat or a small increase traded against faster payment and volume is realistic. No should-cost, so floor unknown.

do: Acknowledge its payment request and our late payments, and commit to pay on time
Recognise past price cuts and improved delivery
Bring verifiable figures, one fresh record per round
Pair each step with a term trade
dont: Ask open questions about its cost or margin

traps: Leaving the cash-discount request unanswered again
Leading with delivery/quality complaints while we pay late
Citing long-span index peaks (not checkable) or unrelated market news like copper or electronics
Demanding a cut against checkable rising steel without data
Asking long payment terms from a cash-seeking supplier
Offering an index clause on rising steel at a generous price
strategy.writer_notes: Open warmly: thank them for steady supply and past price cuts, answer their faster-payment request directly and promise punctual payment. Anchor at the current price, offer faster payment, binding volume and a longer term as the trade. Hold quality and power cost as fresh later arguments. If they cite steel, agree it is real but weigh it by its share of cost. Keep tooling and the exit window unspoken unless they stonewall.

Who on your side signs off price agreements?

findings.text: No should-cost and no competing quotes or RFQs exist for part 330011, so we cannot say how far 181.29 EUR sits above full cost. Any margin judgement rests only on index movements and price history, so the evidence is thin.

The weighted cost drivers argue for a modest increase this year, not a cut. Steel (PPI-C241, weight 0.31) is up 6.5% over 12 months, about +2.0% on the price. Labour (LCI-C, weight 0.27) is up 2.7%, about +0.7%. Power (PPI-D351, weight 0.03) is down 3.7%, about -0.1%. Net, about +2.6% on the 61% of cost covered; the other 39% has no index assigned.

Steel's justification weakens over a longer view. PPI-C241 is still 6.3% below its 2023-08 peak, when the price was 197.70. Since then the price has fallen 8.3% while steel fell about 6% and labour rose about 11%. So the cuts were not purely cost-driven, and margin may already be thinner than in 2023. The longer-span comparisons cannot be checked by the supplier, so they are context only.

Price history: 197.70 (2023), 184.72 (2024, -6.6%), 184.72 (2025), 181.29 (2026, -1.9%). Prices are fixed per calendar year and any change needs 90 days' notice before year end. A 2027 increase request is therefore likely, with the steel rise of +7.8% since 2025-12 as its argument.

Room on price: hold flat at 181.29 against a likely ask of +2 to 3%. Settling at about +1% or below is defensible. A further cut is hard to justify on cost. The supplier has historically settled 2.3 pp below its ask. Its interest in faster payment is a better currency to trade than price.

Faster payment (10 days with cash discount)
risks: Single source with no should-cost; pushing a cut against rising steel may strain a supplier with a 25.6% equity ratio
We pay late on average, which weakens our payment-term position

findings.text: Persona evidence is thin: only two routine e-mails, one noise news item, no call or meeting notes. Decision-makers and approval ladder are unknown. It is a family-owned GmbH (founded 1968, 110 staff, EUR 11.3 M turnover), so decisions are likely short-path, owner-led and relationship-minded. This is an inference, not documented.
Its one explicit ask is cash. On 2026-06-07 it asked us to pay within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount. Faster payment is the currency it values most and a natural trade for price.

It has a legitimate payment grievance. We pay 88.9% of invoices late, 4.3 days after due on average, up to 12 days. Its discount offer has never been used (0 discounts taken). It can raise this if we press on price. We should acknowledge it and offer reliable or faster payment rather than ignore it.

Its finances are sound but not rich. Equity ratio is 25.6% and the credit index is stable at 251 year on year. There is no sign of financial stress, so it can afford to walk away. With a 25.6% equity ratio, a cash request plausibly reflects working-capital preference rather than distress.

Its dependency on us is moderate: our spend of about EUR 384k is roughly 3.4% of its turnover. That share matters to a firm of this size but is not decisive. It is also our single approved source for part 330011, although we own the tooling.

Its style is orderly and planning-focused. It gave advance notice of the holiday shutdown with a call-off deadline (place January call-offs by 10 December). Respecting its planning, and sharing forecasts and binding volume, is likely appreciated.
The ISO 14001 news is noise and gives no lever.

findings.text: Framework agreement ctr:4600070320 covers only part:330011 (Base frame HN 100). Prices are fixed per calendar year. A change needs written notice at least 90 days before year end, i.e. by about 2026-10-02 for 2027. A price increase for 2027 that arrives after that date has no contractual basis.
The term runs 2025-07-01 to 2027-06-30 and auto-extends by 12 months unless terminated with 90 days' notice (by 2027-04-01). Both sides still hold a real exit option.

Commercial terms are payment 30 days net (shorter than our 60-day standard, so already a benefit to them) and DAP with a 28-day lead time. The quality agreement sets a 95% on-time target and a EUR 150 flat fee per supplier-caused complaint.

History shows they settle below their ask. Over 3 renewals the average ask was -0.5% and the average settlement -2.8%. FY2025 asked +3.1% and settled at 0%. The price has fallen from 197.70 (2023) to 181.29 (2026), -8.3%. The flip side is that they have already given a lot, so further cuts get harder.

Dependency is mutual.
- We source the part 100% from them since 2019, with no other approved source and no RFQ, but we own the tooling, so the part can move.
- Our spend of about EUR 384k is about 3.4% of their EUR 11.3M turnover: meaningful but not critical.
- They are financially sound (equity 25.6%, credit index 251 stable, audit grade A), so they can walk away.

Performance against contract: on-time delivery is 88% versus the 95% target, though it improved from 84.6% and is above the peer median. Quality worsened to 949 ppm from 2 complaints versus a 457 ppm peer median; both complaints were recharged and their 8D reports closed.
They asked us to pay within 10 days in exchange for a cash discount, which shows they value cash. Meanwhile we pay on average 4.3 days late, which they can use against us.

findings.text: On-time delivery is below the 95% contract target throughout. It fell from 92.6% (2025Q1) to 80.8% (2025Q4) and has recovered to 88.0% in the rolling 12 months to 2026-09. When deliveries are late, they are late by 11.7 days on average (max 14). On-time against the confirmed date equals on-time against the requested date, so the misses are its own and not a confirmation problem. It is still above the peer median of 84.6%, so it will call itself better than average.

Quality has worsened. The rolling ppm was 0 through 2025Q3 and is 949 now (2 complaints), against a peer median of 457 ppm. Recent complaints are surface damage (qn:20004769) and porosity (qn:20004829); both are supplier-caused and 8D-closed with none overdue. Only EUR 150 was recharged on qn:20004829; the EUR 150 flat fee looks not collected on qn:20004769. Per-lot ppm is jumpy, so we should cite the scorecard figure.

The cost to us is modest in money (2 defective units a year, about 3 late receipts of roughly 12 days each) but real for an A-class single source. It supports asking for an OTD/ppm commitment or a higher chargeback rather than a big price cut. The scorecard still shows class A green (score 89.3), which argues its case.

Volume is stable and predictable. Ordered: about 2,090 pcs in the last 12 months, against a 12-month forecast of 2,160 (+2.7%). The forecast is shared with the supplier and has been reliable (2,040–2,410 range). Summer months are low (110–120 pcs in Jun–Aug 2027). A binding volume or longer term is a tradeable asset: our spend is EUR 384k, about 3.4% of its turnover.
Price history favours the supplier's narrative: 197.70 (2023) → 184.72 (2024–25) → 181.29 (2026), a cumulative -8.3%. It will argue it has already given.

Our own order discipline is mostly fine: confirmations match the requested date on recent POs, and there are 0 stale lines. But there were 5 rush lines and 5 changed lines, which it could cite against us.

arguments.text: Our price has fallen 8.3 % since 2023 (197.70 to 181.29 EUR) while our main cost drivers rose. Steel is about 31 % of our cost and is up 6.5 % in twelve months. Labour is about 27 % and is up 2.7 %. Weighted, that adds roughly 2.7 % to our cost from these two drivers alone. A 2027 adjustment of about +3 % only recovers part of what we have given up.
We have been a fair partner. We cut 6.6 % in 2023 and 1.9 % in 2025, and we held 2025 flat although we had asked for +3.1 %. Further cuts are not sustainable for a family business of 110 people.

Hollerau pays most invoices late: 88.9 % are paid late, by 4.4 days on average. In June we asked for payment within 10 days against a cash discount and got no answer. Our working capital is effectively financing you.

The contract fixes prices per calendar year, and clause 3.1 provides for adjustment with notice. We are giving notice on time, well before 30 September. This is a proper contractual process, not a surprise.
We are a stable, certified source with a long record. We supply 100 % of the HN 100 frame, have supplied the part since 2019, hold ISO 9001 and the new ISO 14001, and rate VDA 6.3 grade A.

weak_points: Delivery is below the 95 % contract target: OTD fell to 80.8-88 % in recent quarters, and the average delay when late is 11.7 days.
ppm has roughly doubled to about 950-1000, with three supplier-caused complaints, including porosity in 2026.
Steel is still 6.3 % below its 2023 peak and 26.7 % below its 2022 high, and power is down 43 % since 2022. They could argue our 2023 price was built on higher costs.
The tooling belongs to Hollerau, so moving the part away from us is easier than it looks.
Our finances are sound (equity ratio 25.6 %, stable credit index), so we cannot plead hardship.
The cash-discount request suggests we value liquidity, which could be used against us.
wants: Payment within 10 days, or at least strictly on time at 30 days; we would grant about 2 % skonto.
A binding annual volume of about 2,100-2,200 pieces with stable call-offs.
A contract extension of 24 months or more beyond 2027-06.
A steel index clause on PPI-C241 instead of a fixed price.
Recognition of the realistic delivery date when we confirm, rather than chargebacks.
red_lines: No further price cut for 2027; flat is the absolute minimum, and only if payment is faster or volume is committed.
No higher complaint chargeback and no tougher ppm penalty without a price offset.
No longer payment terms than 30 days.
No fixed multi-year price without an index clause.
red_team.opening: Thank Hollerau for the long partnership and point to the price cuts we have given since 2023. Give formal notice under clause 3.1 of a +4.5 % increase from 2027-01-01, to about 189.45 EUR, citing steel at +6.5 % with a 31 % share and labour at +2.7 % with a 27 % share. Offer an alternative straight away: +2.5 % if Hollerau pays within 10 days with skonto and commits to binding volume and a 24-month extension, or a steel index clause. Acknowledge the delivery dips and present an improvement plan to pre-empt that counterargument.

rebuttals.answer: You are right that steel and labour have risen and that your price has come down since the first orders; we take both seriously. Put in proportion, though, each driver moves only its own share of your cost: the steel rise, weighted by its share, adds a modest amount, labour adds less, and power has eased over the same twelve months, which offsets a small part. Taken together, the drivers support a smaller adjustment than the one you are asking for. The current price is our reference point, and we would rather close the remaining gap with terms you value than with a straight price rise.

We recognise that you have been a fair partner and that you held prices and cut them over several years; we do not want to squeeze a family business. In the past renewals we have also found common ground below the opening positions, and we would like to do so again. This time we propose to give you something concrete in return: faster payment, a binding volume in line with our shared forecast, and a longer commitment.

This point is fair. We have paid a number of invoices a few days late, and we should have answered your request for faster payment. We apologise for both. We will commit to paying punctually, and we are ready to put shorter payment terms in exchange for the cash discount you offered directly into the agreement. That answers your working-capital concern in a way that costs neither of us a price increase.

We agree that giving notice under the price clause is a proper process, and we appreciate that you are doing so in good time. The clause gives you a right to propose a change, not an automatic increase. The amount still has to be agreed between us on the basis of the facts, and we are happy to do that constructively.

We value the long relationship, your certifications and your audit result, and we want it to continue. Being our sole source also means that reliability carries a lot of weight for us. Delivery performance has improved and is better than many peers, but it is still below the target in our quality agreement, and complaints on this part have risen. We would like to see that improvement continue as part of a balanced agreement, for example through a ppm commitment.

press: We appreciate the improvement in on-time delivery, and we would welcome a plan that brings it up to the target in our quality agreement.
The rolling ppm on the base frame has risen above the peer level, including a porosity complaint, so we would like to agree a ppm target together as part of this renewal.
Power costs have eased over the past twelve months, and we would ask you to reflect that alongside the rises in steel and labour.
Since our shared forecast is slightly above recent orders, we can offer a binding annual volume that gives your plant the planning security it needs.
